**Insiders say Carney government rejected NDP demands before crucial budget vote**
The minority Liberal government led by Prime Minister Mark Carney narrowly survived a crucial confidence vote on November 18, 2025, without making major concessions, despite rejecting the New Democratic Party's (NDP) request for approximately $10 billion in new funding for affordable housing, pharmacare, and other priorities. The NDP sought funding from new revenue and reallocation of spending, including from national defence, which receives nearly $82 billion over five years. **Liberals escape another confidence vote, as opposition complains their methods are 'not sustainable'**
The Canadian federal government survived its fourth confidence vote in under two weeks after the House of Commons passed a ways and means motion to introduce the Budget Implementation Act I, a 600-page bill implementing key measures from the November 4 budget. The motion, tied to budgetary matters, automatically triggered a confidence vote; had it failed, it would have forced the government to resign or call a snap election. The motion passed with a 170-168 vote, narrowly avoiding a potential election during the holiday season. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May provided last-minute support after Prime Minister Mark Carney pledged to uphold the Paris Accord, while four MPs abstained—two Conservative MPs (Matt Jeneroux and Shannon Stubbs) and two New Democrats (Lori Idlout and Gord Johns), with Jeneroux having announced his resignation and Stubbs on medical leave following major jaw and chin surgery. Conservative House leader Andrew Scheer and MP Scott Reid attempted to vote 'no' after the result was known, citing a technical issue with the voting application. Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet expressed relief at avoiding a holiday election and criticized the Liberals' minority strategy as 'not sustainable,' despite his party’s unanimous opposition to the main budget motion. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne stated the government engaged constructively with opposition parties, though opposition leaders argued the government failed to negotiate effectively. Government House leader Steven MacKinnon declined to confirm whether the current approach is sustainable, saying the government would continue advancing policies it believes are in Canada’s long-term interest.
